system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2152-10-06 17:41:00 to 2152-10-15 13:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with chronic abdominal pain, previously attributed to possible chronic pancreatitis or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, was readmitted due to persistent epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had been discharged the day before to attend a gastroenterology follow-up, which resulted in readmission for further evaluation. An MRCP with secretin was performed, showing no evidence of chronic pancreatitis or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, though decreased pancreatic fluid excretion was noted. Her pain was managed with oral hydromorphone and metoclopramide, and she gradually tolerated a soft diet. Presyncope in the ED was attributed to hypovolemia from poor intake. She remained hemodynamically stable, with no signs of acute bleeding or worsening anemia. She was discharged home with continued pain medication and plans for outpatient GI follow-up, as no procedural intervention was recommended at this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. I understand you passed out at your psychologist’s office today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I stood up and everything went dark. I woke up on the floor. I’ve done this before when I’m sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned dizziness and nausea before it happened. Is that part of your usual abdominal pain episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nausea is always there when my stomach pain flares. It’s in my upper left side, worse after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’ve lost about 10 pounds recently without trying?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because I can’t eat much. Every time I do, the pain gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you manage the pain and get your nutrition up. You also had a syncopal episode in the ER two days ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same thing—lightheaded, then blacked out. I didn’t hit my head either time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, no injury. We did a chest X-ray to check for anything serious. It was clear—no pneumonia or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a cold lately, but it’s mild. Is that why I fainted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. When you’re dehydrated or not eating well, standing up can drop your blood pressure. That, plus a mild URI, could explain it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. Your vitals are stable. We’ll keep an IV for fluids and start pain meds to help you eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to some pain meds, like hydromorphone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll avoid those. We’ll use alternatives and monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. I had some toast and kept it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep encouraging small meals. Your urine test came back—no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about a UTI. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and no signs of bleeding or anemia worsening. We’ll keep checking your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well with oral intake, but you’re still not eating like at home. Your GI doctor wants you to stay until you’re back to your baseline diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to go home, but I know I’m not ready. The pain’s still there, just less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focused on getting you stable. We also need to make sure the fainting doesn’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sitting up slowly. No dizziness yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep doing that. We’ll continue IV fluids until you’re eating enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reviewing your recent MRCP again with radiology to make sure we didn’t miss anything with your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many scans. None have shown clear pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Some show decreased pancreatic fluid, but no definite chronic pancreatitis. We’re considering other causes for your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be something else? My stomach just feels so sensitive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re looking at biliary tract issues too. But for now, we’re managing symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two days of improved intake. That’s great. But you’re still losing weight unintentionally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m trying. I just don’t have an appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a PICC line tomorrow so we can start nutritional support through the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me gain weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it will give your body the calories and nutrients it needs while your stomach heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just got confirmation—the PICC line will be placed tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very. It’s a small tube in your arm vein, guided by ultrasound. We’ll check with a chest X-ray after to make sure it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully this morning. The chest X-ray shows it’s in the right position—tip in the SVC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel a thing. Is the nutrition starting now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting parenteral nutrition. It will help you regain strength and weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. This will help with that. We’ll monitor your labs closely for any imbalances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. You’ve had three meals today without nausea. Pain is mild.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually felt hungry this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. We’ll keep the PICC for now, but you’re on track to go home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do you think?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow, if you keep this up. We’ll make sure you can eat consistently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Any dizziness when standing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’ve been careful. I feel much more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. That means your hydration and nutrition are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had another good day with meals. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What about the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will stay in for now. You’ll get home nutrition support and follow up with GI and nutrition services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to come back for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for monitoring and eventual removal. We’ll coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue managing it with safe meds. Your GI doctor will review imaging again and may suggest next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fainting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As long as you stay hydrated and eat regularly, it’s unlikely to return. But if it happens again, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep up with the diet, take meds as prescribed, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad I didn’t hit my head when I fell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and no new injuries. Just take it slow when standing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing that. No dizziness at all today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re ready to go home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m feeling hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best sign of all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my left breast has been sore for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lump, you said? And it’s not worse with movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lump, and it’s constant. Not painful, just uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll note it. Please follow up with your PCP for a breast exam, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s what we’re here for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my hearing—I read lips, so I catch most of what you say.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure to face you and speak clearly. Your care team knows about your hearing loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. It makes a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want you to understand everything. Take your time going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with chronic abdominal pain and a history of syncope was admitted after fainting at her psychologist’s office, with a second syncopal episode noted in the ER two days prior. Her abdominal pain, localized to the left upper quadrant and worsened by eating, had led to a 10-pound unintentional weight loss and poor oral intake. She was admitted for pain control, nutritional support, and evaluation of recurrent syncope. A chest X-ray showed no acute disease, and urine culture revealed no infection. A PICC line was placed on hospital day 6 to initiate parenteral nutrition, supporting gradual improvement in oral intake and weight stabilization. She regained strength, tolerated a regular diet, and remained free of dizziness or syncope before discharge. Follow-up was arranged for ongoing GI evaluation, PICC line management, and assessment of persistent left breast pain. She was discharged home in stable condition with a plan for outpatient care.
